newsitem.title: UK: UK motor trade seeks 1997 car registration change.
newsitem.headline: UK motor trade seeks 1997 car registration change.

text.p: Trade bodies representing the British car retail industry said on Tuesday that they hoped to persuade the government to change the way cars are registered by 1997.

Ernie Thompson, chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) told reporters at the British International Motor Show that the practise of changing annual car registration letters in August created enormous imbalances in demand and was "a huge add-on cost to the industry".
Every August demand in Britain rises to around 500,000 cars, or a quarter of annual sales, as buyers seek to take the chance to get the new registration letter as soon as it is available.
Alan Pulham, director of the National Franchise Dealers Association, said "we are determined to get a change in 1997."
"We now at last seem to have some elements of the government accepting the logic of what we're asking for," he added.

The SMMT said Transport Secretary Sir George Young had promised to look into changing the format of registrations and accepted that the "August bulge" created huge supply, stocking and delivery problems.
However, the SMMT's Thompson admitted that the costs of changing registration practises were a major deterrent for the government.
The August registration change was originally set up to stimulate the once sleepy British summer car market.
Among its strongest supporters are police forces who fear that alternative systems will produce longer, less memorable letter and number sequences that will make crime detection harder.
